finalText:
**Merge** creates a commit that joins two branches together, keeping all the history of both sides. You end up with a commit graph that shows "here's where we split, here's where we came back." It's the safe choice for shared branches because it doesn't rewrite history.

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the branch you're rebasing onto, as if you'd written them there from the start. You get a straight line of commits instead of a fork and rejoin. It rewrites history, so it's not safe to do on branches other people are using.

The practical rule: **rebase for your own work before you push it; merge for work that's already shared.**

Use rebase when you've been working on a feature branch and want to tidy up before opening a pull request — it keeps your PR's history clean and easy to review. Use merge when you're integrating branches (like merging a feature into main, or main back into a long-running branch) — people may have built work on top of those branches, so rewriting their history breaks things.

A smaller rebase use case: if you're syncing with main while still on your branch, rebase keeps your commits stacked on top of the latest main instead of creating a merge commit every time. But if the branch is shared, merge instead.

The one gotcha: never force-push a rebase unless you're absolutely sure you're the only one using that branch.
